subject: feminism
title: The Awakening Foundation (婦女新知基金會): a tiny advocacy group that rewrote Taiwan's family and work laws
dek: Awakening began in 1982 as a feminist magazine published under martial law and became a foundation in 1987 with a fund of just NT$600,000. With six or seven paid staff and a volunteer board, it drafted or co-drafted many of the laws Taiwanese women now take for granted, from the Gender Equality in Employment Act to the rewritten family chapters of the Civil Code. In 2025 its whole income was about NT$5.7 million, roughly one hundred-and-tenth of Garden of Hope's. This second lesson in the Taiwan organization series explains what an advocacy organization does, how it is funded, how to read its very short financial statements, and what a small shop like cool dairy could mean to it.
era: 1982 to the present: the Awakening magazine under martial law, the 1987 foundation, the law-reform campaigns of the 1990s and 2000s, partnership and marriage equality after 2009, and the 2025 work report and financial statements
honesty: This lesson is text only. The history comes from the Awakening Foundation's own pages (its introduction, founding story and year-by-year chronicle), the English Wikipedia articles on the foundation and on Lee Yuan-chen, and the earlier lesson on Taiwan's women's movement. All money figures are copied from the foundation's 2025 financial statements, and the 2025 activities from its 2025 work report, both published on its website in March 2026. Where the foundation's own chronicle is the only source, the lesson says so, and where the statements leave something unexplained, the lesson says that too instead of guessing. This is a study guide, not legal or financial advice: before cool dairy signs a partnership, confirm the details with the organization and, if needed, an accountant.

timeline.label: Annette Lu is jailed
timeline.detail: After the Kaohsiung Incident in December 1979, Annette Lu, who had started Taiwan's 'New Feminism' in the 1970s, is arrested and imprisoned. Her friends in the women's movement have to find a new way to keep working.

timeline.label: Awakening magazine
timeline.detail: Lee Yuan-chen and a group of feminists found the Awakening magazine publishing house (婦女新知雜誌社), which the foundation describes as Taiwan's first feminist magazine. Taiwan is still under martial law.

timeline.label: Abortion petition
timeline.detail: Awakening rallies seven women's groups to send a statement signed by 154 women to the Legislative Yuan, pushing for the Genetic Health Act (優生保健法), which legalized abortion under set conditions that year.

timeline.label: From magazine to foundation
timeline.detail: Martial law ends in July. Awakening raises a fund of NT$600,000 and registers as the Awakening Foundation in October, according to its own founding page. The same year it joins thirty-two groups protesting the trafficking of girls and starts drafting an equal employment bill.

timeline.label: Equal employment bill
timeline.detail: Awakening finishes its draft Equal Employment Bill for men and women and holds a public hearing. It will take twelve years to pass.

timeline.label: Kaohsiung association
timeline.detail: The Kaohsiung Awakening Association (高雄市婦女新知協會) is founded, a membership organization that works alongside the foundation.

timeline.label: Civil law hotline
timeline.detail: Awakening trains its first volunteers and opens a free telephone hotline giving legal advice on marriage and family law. The same year it supports Deng Ru-wen and organizes the 22 May march against sexual harassment.

timeline.label: The 新晴 draft
timeline.detail: With the Taipei Warm Life Association for Women (晚晴婦女協會), Awakening carries a draft rewrite of the family chapters of the Civil Code, backed by 30,000 signatures, into the Legislative Yuan.

timeline.label: Custody reform and a night march
timeline.detail: The Legislative Yuan removes the rule that gave fathers priority in child custody. After the murder of Peng Wan-ru on 30 November, Awakening co-organizes the 21 December night march for women's safety.

timeline.label: Employment equality passes
timeline.detail: After twelve years, the Gender Equality in Employment Act (then 兩性工作平等法) passes its third reading. It takes effect on 8 March 2002.

timeline.label: Gender equity in schools
timeline.detail: As part of a civil-society alliance, Awakening helps pass the Gender Equity Education Act.

timeline.label: Partnership rights alliance
timeline.detail: Awakening co-founds the Taiwan Alliance to Promote Civil Partnership Rights (伴侶盟) with LGBTQ groups. In 2011 the alliance publishes a civil-society draft of partnership and marriage laws.

timeline.label: Campaign against the adultery crime
timeline.detail: Awakening launches a petition to repeal Article 239 of the Criminal Code, which made adultery a crime. The Constitutional Court struck the article down in 2020.

timeline.label: One-third rule for local councils
timeline.detail: On 21 November 2025 the Local Government Act is amended so that the old reserved quota of one-quarter of seats for women becomes a one-third gender-ratio rule. Awakening had campaigned for it with other women's groups since January.

sections.title: Before Awakening: feminism without an organization

blocks.text: In the 1970s Taiwan was a one-party state under martial law. Political parties other than the Kuomintang were banned, and so were most independent associations. Annette Lu's 'New Feminism' gave the idea of women's equality a public voice, through essays, talks and a small publishing house, but it was carried by individuals rather than by a lasting organization. When Lu was arrested after the Kaohsiung Incident of December 1979, the movement lost its best-known speaker.

Lee Yuan-chen, a scholar of Chinese literature who later became a professor at Tamkang University, had her own reason to care about family law. After her divorce in 1973 she lost custody of her daughter, because the Civil Code of the time gave fathers priority. She and a group of women who had worked with Lu decided that the movement needed something that could survive the arrest of any one person. Under martial law, the safest form for that was a magazine.

The earlier lesson on Taiwan's women's movement told this story from the point of view of the whole movement. This lesson follows one organization through it, because the question for cool dairy is not only what happened but who is still doing the work today and how they pay for it.

sections.title: 1982 to 1987: a magazine that turned into a foundation

blocks.text: The Awakening magazine (婦女新知) began publishing in 1982. Its aim, in the founders' words, was to awaken women's self-awareness, fight for women's rights and promote gender equality. Besides the magazine, the group ran public events. In 1983 it held a week of activities called the 8338 Women's Week, built around International Women's Day on 8 March, which the foundation says drew many women into women's organizations. In 1984 it collected the signatures of 154 women and sent them, with seven women's groups, to the Legislative Yuan in support of legal abortion, which became part of the Genetic Health Act that year.

The magazine was always short of money. Martial law was lifted in July 1987, and in October Awakening raised a fund of NT$600,000 and registered as a foundation, a 財團法人. A foundation could receive donations more easily, invite experts onto a board, and act as a permanent headquarters for campaigns. The NT$600,000 is still on the books today: the 2025 balance sheet lists exactly NT$600,000 as 'permanently restricted net assets', the founding fund that the foundation may not spend.

The first campaigns of the foundation show its style. In 1987 it backed the women who worked as guides at the National Dr. Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall, who were required to resign when they turned thirty or became pregnant. In 1988 it held three protests against beauty pageants, which it said displayed women like goods in a competition, and it marched with the Taiwan Women's Rescue Foundation on Huaxi Street against child prostitution, the same campaign that produced Garden of Hope. It also began reviewing school textbooks for gender stereotypes.

sections.title: How an advocacy organization works: draft the law, then fight for it

blocks.text: Garden of Hope, from last week's lesson, is mainly a service provider: it runs shelters, counseling and job training, often under government contracts. Awakening is mainly an advocacy organization. Its product is not a service delivered to a client but a change in the rules that affect everyone. Its method, repeated over four decades, has five parts.

items: Find the problem in real cases. The civil law hotline, opened in 1994, gives free legal advice on marriage and family problems, and the foundation says it handles more than two thousand calls a year. The hotline has published yearly reports since 1995 on what callers ask about, which tells the foundation which laws hurt women in practice.

Write the bill yourself. Awakening drafted its Equal Employment Bill in 1989 and kept revising it, reaching a fifth version in 1995 that added a chapter on workplace sexual harassment and a sixth in 1998. With the Warm Life Association it wrote its own version of the Civil Code's family chapters.
Show public support. In 1995 the Civil Code draft went to the Legislative Yuan with 30,000 signatures. In 1999 volunteers gathered signatures for the employment bill outside Taipei Main Station.

Lobby and watch. Awakening organized a 'grandmothers and mothers lobbying team' (婆婆媽媽遊說團) in 1995 to follow the Civil Code bill through the legislature, and a 'grandmothers and mothers court-watching team' in 1998 to observe how judges handled family cases. Before elections it asks candidates to sign pledges and publishes how legislators voted.

Check the law after it passes. The foundation regularly holds press conferences that review a law some years after it took effect, such as the 2009 five-year review of the Gender Equity Education Act and the 2016 four-year review of the Family Act (家事事件法).

blocks.text: This method is slow. The employment bill took twelve years, from the 1989 draft to its passage in 2001. The rewrite of the rules on marital property took about eleven years. The campaign against the crime of adultery began with a petition in 2013 and ended only when the Constitutional Court struck the law down in 2020. An advocacy group's results come years after the donations that paid for them, and they are shared with many other groups, which makes them hard to count.

The foundation's own introduction and chronicle list the laws it helped pass, often in coalition with other groups. Each of them is a separate story, but together they show how much of Taiwan's legal framework for gender equality passed through this one small office.

items: Body and safety: the Genetic Health Act of 1984, which legalized abortion under conditions; the reform of the sexual offences chapter of the Criminal Code in 1999; and the Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Prevention Acts.

Family: the rewritten family chapters of the Civil Code, including the 1996 removal of fathers' priority in custody, new marital property rules in the early 2000s, and the 2007 change allowing parents to agree on whether a child takes the father's or the mother's surname; and the Family Act, which passed in December 2011 after a draft group the foundation set up in 1999.
Work: the Gender Equality in Employment Act of 2001, which covers equal treatment, sexual harassment at work and parental leave; it has been renamed since and is now called 性別平等工作法.
School: the Gender Equity Education Act of 2004, passed with a wider civil-society alliance.

Migrants: amendments to the Immigration Act in 2007 that protected women who came to Taiwan through marriage, pushed by the Alliance for Human Rights Legislation for Immigrants and Migrants, which Awakening helped start in 2003.
Government: a law passed in 2010 created a Department of Gender Equality inside the Executive Yuan, which the foundation had demanded since the early 2000s; the department opened in 2012.

Partnership and marriage: Awakening co-founded the partnership rights alliance in 2009, which wrote a civil-society draft of partnership and same-sex marriage laws in 2011. The Constitutional Court's Interpretation 748 in May 2017 and the same-sex marriage law of 2019 followed.

blocks.text: The foundation also published practical handbooks for women, such as the 'Complete Guide to Leaving Home' series on marital property, divorce and marital violence (女人完全逃家手冊, 1996 and 1997), a handbook against sexual harassment, a guide to cultural sensitivity toward new immigrants, and 《做親密，愛自主》, a booklet on affirmative consent. In 2001 it made a documentary on sexual harassment, 《玫瑰的戰爭》 ('The War of the Roses'), and screened it at nearly a hundred campuses.

The 2025 work report is a short table organized by the foundation's working groups. It shows an organization that mostly issues statements, attends press conferences, writes reports for government reviews and trains volunteers. The main items are:

items: Marriage and family: work on divorce law reform, including two press conferences, one on Mother's Day on 8 May about the economic independence of divorced mothers and one on 29 August, with the Judicial Reform Foundation, asking why the legislature had still not reformed divorce law after a 2023 Constitutional Court ruling.

Body autonomy: statements on the bill to reform the Assisted Reproduction Act and allow surrogacy, which the foundation wants handled separately and carefully; three campus talks on affirmative consent; a speech at the Taiwan Transgender March in November.

Care and economic security: statements against forcing women to take longer maternity leave, in favor of flexible parental leave with better support, and against relaxing the rules for hiring foreign domestic workers as a solution to women's careers.

Labor: a workplace gender-equality advice line with five newly trained volunteers and an average satisfaction score of 4.5 out of 5; a statement on Equal Pay Day; screenings of a documentary about the Golden Crane (金鶴) women workers.

Politics: the campaign that ended on 21 November 2025, when the Local Government Act changed the one-quarter quota of seats reserved for women in local councils into a one-third gender-ratio rule; statements criticizing sexist remarks by politicians of several parties; and a shadow report for Taiwan's fifth national report under CEDAW, the UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women.

Democratic defence: a project funded by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, a German political foundation, with workshops on civil defence and information warfare and a policy paper on 'resilient and inclusive whole-of-society defence', presented on 25 November.
Training: legal courses for hotline volunteers, 18 office volunteers, 13 interns across the year, and two student assistants who wrote reports on local gender-equality committees.

blocks.text: Notice what is missing compared with Garden of Hope: there are no shelters, no case numbers in the tens of thousands, and no service sites. The hotlines are the only direct services. Almost everything else is research, writing and public pressure.

sections.title: Where the money comes from and where it goes

blocks.text: The foundation posts its budget, work report and financial statements every year on a page called 財務徵信, 'financial verification'. The 2025 statements were signed by the chair, Hung Hui-fen (洪惠芬). In 2025 total income was NT$5,747,260, made up of:

items: Donations: NT$3,260,148, or 57 percent.
Government subsidies: NT$2,226,438, or 39 percent.
Interest: NT$176,666, or 3 percent.
Sales of goods and services, such as publications and donation gifts: NT$53,904, or 1 percent.
Other income: NT$30,104, or 1 percent.

blocks.text: Total spending was NT$8,049,523, so the foundation ran a deficit of about NT$2.3 million and drew on its reserves. At the end of 2025 its net assets were NT$11,847,156, of which NT$600,000 is the permanent founding fund. In other words, Awakening has savings worth roughly a year and a half of spending.

The year before looked very different. In 2024 income was NT$8,891,638, of which donations were NT$7,768,625, or 87 percent, and government subsidies only NT$795,818. Donations fell by NT$4.5 million between the two years. The statements do not say why, so this lesson does not guess. For a small organization, a single large gift or one campaign year can move the totals a great deal.

Two more details are worth noticing, because they show how to read a financial statement. First, the balance sheet lists NT$7,058,674 of 'income received in advance' (預收款項) at the end of 2025, up from NT$384,500. This is money that has arrived but belongs to work in a later period, so accountants count it as a liability rather than as income. Second, the split between program spending and administrative spending flipped: in 2024 program spending was NT$6,104,411 and administration NT$898,890, but in 2025 program spending was NT$1,530,896 and administration NT$6,518,627. The statement gives no explanation. The likeliest reason is a change in how staff costs were classified, but that is a guess, and the right thing to do as a possible partner is to ask.

Compare the scale with Garden of Hope, whose 2025 income was about NT$640.7 million. Awakening's income was less than one percent of that. A donation of NT$50,000 from cool dairy would be a rounding error for Garden of Hope but nearly one percent of Awakening's whole year, and about one and a half percent of its donations.

sections.title: Foundation, association, alliance: three ways to organize

blocks.text: Awakening is a 財團法人, a foundation. Under Taiwan's Foundations Act (財團法人法), a foundation is built around a fund of property and run by a board. Awakening's board members are experts on gender issues who serve without pay, and the board hires a small paid staff, which the foundation describes as six or seven people. The Foundations Act requires foundations to report their budgets and accounts to the government, and Awakening also publishes its own on its website.

The Kaohsiung Awakening Association, founded in 1992, and a Taipei association are different legal creatures: they are 社團法人, associations built around members who elect their own officers. They share the Awakening name and work with the foundation, but they are separate organizations. If cool dairy wants to support Awakening's work in the south, for example, it would be dealing with a different legal body from the one in Taipei.

Much of Awakening's work also happens through alliances: the partnership rights alliance with LGBTQ groups, the immigrant rights alliance, alliances on childcare and long-term care, and joint press conferences with many women's groups. This is efficient for a tiny organization, but it means that a single victory usually belongs to several groups at once.

sections.title: What was happening elsewhere at the same time

blocks.text: Awakening's founding years overlapped with several turning points in other countries' women's movements:

items: United States, 1982. The deadline for ratifying the Equal Rights Amendment expired on 30 June 1982, the same year Awakening's magazine began. American feminists turned to state laws and court cases, while Taiwan's feminists were just starting to build organizations.

Japan, 1985. Japan's Equal Employment Opportunity Law passed in May 1985 and took effect in April 1986. Critics said it mostly asked employers to 'make efforts' rather than forbidding discrimination, and many companies responded with a two-track hiring system. Taiwan's own employment equality bill, drafted by Awakening in 1989, took until 2001 and was written to be stronger.

South Korea, 1987. Korean Women's Associations United was founded in February 1987, in the same year that both Korea and Taiwan moved toward democracy. Like Awakening, it combined the women's movement with the democracy movement and later pushed for laws against sexual violence.

blocks.text: The common pattern in Taiwan and South Korea is that feminist organizations grew up together with democratization, so their main tool became law reform through newly elected legislatures. That history still shapes Awakening today: it thinks of itself as a watchdog of government as much as a women's group.
Here is a plain summary to set beside last week's notes on Garden of Hope.

items: Strengths: forty-four years of history and a record of laws that every Taiwanese woman lives under; it publishes its work reports and financial statements; it is independent and criticizes politicians of every party; and its issues, from divorce law to care work and body autonomy, fit a shop that wants to educate customers about women's rights.

Things to weigh: it is small and its income swings a lot from year to year; its 2025 accounts show a deficit and an unexplained change in how spending is classified; and its results are changes in law that take years and are shared with coalitions, so cool dairy cannot point to 'one shelter bed' or 'one girl helped'.

What a small donor means: a few tens of thousands of NT dollars is a real share of Awakening's budget. It could pay for a hotline volunteer training course or a campaign's printing costs. That makes it possible to tell customers a concrete story, if the foundation agrees to say what the money paid for.

Easy first steps: the foundation lists a charity code for electronic receipts, 愛心碼 3899, so shoppers in Taiwan can donate the lottery chance on their e-invoice to it. Cool dairy could print that code on its packaging before signing any formal partnership.

Questions to ask before partnering: Why did donations fall from about NT$7.8 million in 2024 to about NT$3.3 million in 2025? Why did administrative spending rise from about NT$0.9 million to about NT$6.5 million? What is the NT$7 million received in advance for? Can a donation be earmarked for one working group, such as the marriage and family law hotline? How does the foundation thank and report to small business donors?

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Awakening's victories, such as equal custody rights or the one-third rule for local councils, help millions of women but cannot be counted per donated dollar. Garden of Hope's shelters help fewer people but can be counted exactly. If cool dairy splits its donations between one service organization and one advocacy organization, how would you explain that choice to a customer in two sentences on the shop's About page?

fun_fact.title: Grandmothers, mothers and a sunny draft
fun_fact.text: Two of Awakening's best-known campaign names are deliberately homely. In 1995 it organized a 婆婆媽媽遊說團, a 'grandmothers and mothers lobbying team', to follow the Civil Code bill through the Legislative Yuan, and in 1998 a 婆婆媽媽法院觀察團 to sit in court and watch how judges treated women in family cases. The Civil Code draft they were pushing was called the 新晴版, the 'new clear sky' version: its name joins the 新 of 婦女新知 with the 晴 of its partner, the 晚晴婦女協會, and reads like a promise of better weather for married women.

glossary.explain: 財團法人婦女新知基金會, a feminist advocacy foundation in Taipei. It began as a magazine in 1982 and registered as a foundation in 1987.
The feminist magazine founded in 1982 under martial law, which the foundation calls Taiwan's first. It later became a newsletter (通訊).
Born 1946, a scholar of Chinese literature at Tamkang University who led the founding of Awakening in 1982 and its conversion into a foundation in 1987.
The lawyer and writer who launched Taiwan's 'New Feminism' in the 1970s. She was jailed after the 1979 Kaohsiung Incident and later became Vice President (2000–2008).
A pro-democracy rally in Kaohsiung on 10 December 1979 that ended in clashes and the arrest of opposition leaders, including Annette Lu.
The emergency rule in force in Taiwan from 1949 to July 1987, which banned opposition parties and limited free association and the press.
A week of events Awakening held in 1983 around International Women's Day on 8 March.
The 1984 law that made abortion legal under set conditions in Taiwan. Awakening petitioned for it.
A foundation: a legal body built around a fund of property and run by a board. Governed since 2018 by the Foundations Act (財團法人法).
An association: a legal body built around members who elect its officers. The Taipei and Kaohsiung Awakening associations take this form.
The 2018 law that sets the rules for Taiwan's foundations, including the duty of government-funded foundations to report budgets and accounts.
A membership association founded in 1992 that works alongside the foundation in southern Taiwan.
Awakening's free telephone advice service on marriage and family law, staffed by trained volunteers since 1994.
Awakening's draft law on equality at work, first finished in 1989 and revised many times until a version passed in 2001.
The 2001 law, in force from 8 March 2002, that bans sex discrimination at work and covers sexual harassment and parental leave. It has since been renamed.
The 2004 law requiring gender equality education in schools and gender equity committees in schools and governments.
The part of Taiwan's Civil Code that governs marriage, custody, property between spouses and surnames. Awakening campaigned to rewrite it from the 1990s on.
The 1995 civil-society draft of the Civil Code family chapters written by Awakening and the Warm Life Association for Women.
A Taipei women's group supporting divorced and separated women. It co-wrote the 1995 新晴 draft with Awakening.
Awakening's 1995 volunteer team that followed the Civil Code bill through the Legislative Yuan.
A woman who killed her abusive husband in 1993. Awakening supported her in 1994, and her case helped lead to the 1998 Domestic Violence Prevention Act.
A feminist leader and director of the Democratic Progressive Party's women's department who was murdered in Kaohsiung on 30 November 1996.
The law on court procedures for family cases, passed in December 2011. Awakening began drafting proposals for it in 1999.

glossary.term: Taiwan Alliance to Promote Civil Partnership Rights
glossary.explain: An alliance founded in 2009 by Awakening and LGBTQ groups, which in 2011 published a civil-society draft of partnership and marriage laws.
The Constitutional Court ruling of 24 May 2017 that the Civil Code's exclusion of same-sex couples from marriage was unconstitutional.
The article of the Criminal Code that made adultery a crime. Awakening campaigned against it from 2013, and the Constitutional Court struck it down in 2020.
The office inside the Executive Yuan responsible for gender equality policy, created by a 2010 law and opened in 2012.
The law that organizes Taiwan's local governments. Its amendment on 21 November 2025 replaced the one-quarter quota of seats for women with a one-third gender-ratio rule.

aliases: Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women
glossary.explain: The UN treaty on women's rights. Taiwan applies it through domestic law and holds national report reviews, for which groups like Awakening write shadow reports.
A report by civil-society groups that answers a government's official report to a treaty review, pointing out problems the government left out.

aliases: 弗里德里希諾曼自由基金會
glossary.explain: A German political foundation linked to the liberal Free Democratic Party that funds projects abroad. It funded Awakening's 2025 democratic defence project.
An organization whose main work is changing laws, policies and public opinion rather than providing services to individuals.
The page where a Taiwanese charity publishes its budgets, reports and accounts so donors can check them.
Money a body has received for work in a later period. Accountants record it as a liability until the work is done.
Assets a foundation may never spend, such as its founding fund. Awakening's is NT$600,000.
A code that lets shoppers donate their electronic invoice, and its lottery chance, to a registered charity. Awakening's is 3899.
A large Christian-rooted foundation founded in 1988 that runs services against gender-based violence. The subject of the previous lesson in this series.
A proposed amendment to the US Constitution guaranteeing equal rights regardless of sex. Its ratification deadline expired on 30 June 1982.
Japan's equal employment law, passed in May 1985 and in force from April 1986, criticized for relying on employers' voluntary efforts.
An umbrella body of South Korean women's groups founded in February 1987, during Korea's democratization.
Awakening's documentary on sexual harassment, shown at nearly a hundred campuses in 2001.
Awakening's handbook series of 1996 and 1997 on marital property, divorce and marital violence.
Chair of the Awakening Foundation's board, who signed the 2025 financial statements.
